title: Working for Frank Painia and why he changed bands
summary: Short stints at the Dew Drop; staying too long creates a rut.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I think I'd ask you about, we talked about the Doudrop. Did you, and you must have known Frank Panyang.
Did you do a lot of work for Frank?
I mean I know he had other venues that he put.
Well see now the same thing with the Doudrop. I didn't stay there too long. I was there a lot of times. I never would stay there no more than a few months. Then I'd leave and then come back.

And I'll tell you another reason why I changed bands like that. Once you stay with one band too long, you play the same music all the time, you get in a rut. You get in a rut. You don't find yourself improving yourself.
So you don't find it that it's a challenge, that the music's not as challenging? What? When you stay with one band for a long time.

No, because as far as reading the music, once you play it over a couple of times, you know, looking at it, you can memorize it anyway. And it slows you up on your reading. But every time you get something new that you've never seen before.
